name: Single Point Charge
text: A single point charge creates a simple electric field pattern. The field lines radiate outward from a positive charge or inward toward a negative charge, forming a symmetrical pattern around the charge.This pattern is easy to recognize and serves as the foundation for understanding more complex field arrangements. The strength of the field decreases as you move away from the charge.

images.alt: Single Point Charge. A single charge creates a radial electric field.

name: Two Like Charges
text: For two equal positive charges, field lines point away from both charges and curve away from the region between them. The lines themselves do not repel; the net field is the vector sum of the two fields. At the midpoint, the equal and opposite contributions cancel, so the net field is zero.

images.alt: Two Like Charges. For equal positive charges, the midpoint has zero net electric field.

name: Two Opposite Charges (Dipole)
text: A dipole consists of equal positive and negative charges. Field lines start on the positive charge and end on the negative charge. Between the charges, both contributions point from positive to negative and reinforce each other. The field becomes very strong close to either charge.

images.alt: Two Opposite Charges (Dipole). Dipole field lines run from the positive charge to the negative charge.

name: Multiple Charges (Complex)
text: With three or more charges, the electric field pattern becomes much more complicated. Field lines twist and curve as they respond to the influence of each charge in the system.These complex patterns are found in real-world scenarios, such as in atoms or charged objects. Understanding the basics helps you interpret these more advanced diagrams.

images.alt: Multiple Charges (Complex). The net field combines the vector contributions of all source charges.
